title: That’s Impossible!
lead: God’s promises are not limited by human possibilities.
questions: Who do you speak about more harshly than God would speak about them, and what would change if you quoted them as gently as the Lord quoted Sarah?
Who near you listens to promises with a stony face because they have been burned by waiting, and how can you be with them without condemnation?
What could you start doing this year even though only the next generation will benefit from it, and what is holding you back?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: Almost a quarter of a century has passed since God’s call in yesterday’s reading. Abraham is ninety-nine years old, and Sarah not much younger. And just then, in the hottest part of the day, three travelers appear in front of the tent. The old man runs, hurries everyone along, promises “a bit of bread,” and then lays out a feast of fine flour and a choice calf. That is the mark of generous people: they promise a fraction of what they give. Abraham doesn’t yet know that he is hosting God.

Then comes the sentence this household has waited years to hear: by this time next year Sarah will have a son. Behind the Guest’s back, the woman listens and laughs. Not out loud: “she laughed to herself.” It isn’t mockery of God. It is the reflex of someone whom life has taught not to grab hold of hope. And the Guest hears a laugh that made no sound, and that is how the hosts recognize who is sitting at their table.

There is also a detail that says more about God than many a psalm. Sarah described herself with a word used for a worn-out garment, and added that her husband was old: “After I am worn out and my master is old…” When God repeats her thought to Abraham, all He says is: “Can I really bear a child when I am old?” God speaks of us more gently than we speak of ourselves.

The Guest answers the laughter with a question that will echo throughout the Bible: “Is anything too difficult for the LORD?” Frightened, Sarah denies that she laughed, and He closes the conversation: “No… but you did laugh.” It sounds like being caught out, but it is a promise: since you laughed against hope, you will give birth against nature. God doesn’t reject Sarah because her faith wavered, and He doesn’t take back the promise. A real, wounded laugh is enough for Him.

“The LORD attended to Sarah as He had said, and the LORD did for Sarah what He had promised.” God gives the child the name Isaac, which means “he laughs.” Every time Sarah calls her son, she will say a word that recalls that laugh behind the tent flap. God didn’t erase her unbelief. He transformed it: the laughter of despair became the laughter of joy. Later Abraham plants a tamarisk in Beersheba, a slow-growing tree for the generations to come, and calls God the Eternal. Sometimes hope looks as unimpressive as a seedling in dry ground.

Almost a quarter of a century has passed since God’s call in yesterday’s reading. In that time the promise of a son was repeated, made more specific, and sealed with a covenant. And nothing. What’s more, between chapters sixteen and seventeen of this story, between one line and the next, thirteen years go by in which God doesn’t say a word. The man of the promise traveled most of his road in silence. Abraham is ninety-nine years old, and Sarah not much younger. The promise has grown old along with them. Today’s story begins in the hottest part of the day, when no one expects anything anymore, and it ends with a child being given a name that means laughter.

sections.heading: A Guest in the Heat of the Day
paragraphs: “Then the LORD appeared to Abraham by the Oaks of Mamre in the heat of the day, while he was sitting at the entrance of his tent.” Noon in the Middle East is the time when life comes to a standstill. Everyone takes cover in the shade, and the roads empty. And right then, resting, Abraham looks up and sees three travelers.

From there things move very quickly. A man of nearly a hundred hurries out to meet them, then dashes into the tent, hurries Sarah along, and runs to the herd. The sentences are short and clipped, as if the narrator himself were out of breath. And in all this bustle there is one more trait by which you can recognize generous people: Abraham promises his guests “a bit of bread,” and then has three measures of the finest flour kneaded and picks “a tender and choice calf” from the herd. A feast for three that a king would not be ashamed of. That is how generous people talk: they promise a fraction of what they intend to give.

There is one more line in this welcome worth remembering for later. “Let a little water be brought, that you may wash your feet.” In the Middle East a host offered guests water, but did not wash their feet himself. That was a slave’s job. When, two thousand years later, Someone at a table takes a basin and kneels at His disciples’ feet Himself, He will cross a line that even generous Abraham did not cross.

The patriarch doesn’t yet know who his guest is. He serves the meal, stands off to the side under the tree like a servant, and watches them eat. God accepted a meal from his hand. Before a word is said about a son, something unheard of happens: the Most High sits in the shade of a tree at someone else’s table and eats. It is a foreshadowing of Someone who, two thousand years later, would eat with ordinary people, even with tax collectors.

This meal is also remembered in the Letter to the Hebrews. When, many centuries later, its author tells his readers to remember hospitality, because by it “some people have entertained angels without knowing it,” he is recalling this very noon under the oaks of Mamre. No one ever knows whom they are really letting into their home.

sections.heading: Laughter Behind the Tent Flap
paragraphs: During that meal comes the sentence this household has waited a quarter of a century to hear: “I will surely return to you at this time next year, and your wife Sarah will have a son!” Sarah hears it at the entrance to the tent, behind the Guest’s back. And she laughs. Not out loud; the text says clearly: “she laughed to herself.” It was an inner laugh, inaudible, locked inside her thoughts.

Before anyone judges that laugh, a reminder: Sarah wasn’t the first. A year earlier, when God announced the same thing to Abraham, he fell facedown and laughed too, asking himself whether a son could be born to a man of a hundred. The father of faith had already laughed at this promise before his wife ever heard it. Those who laughed at this announcement were to become the parents of the promised child. God knew that, and He didn’t change His plans.

Let’s stay with Sarah’s laugh a moment before we judge it. Abraham’s wife had lived for decades with a promise that didn’t come true. She had traveled a long road from hope, through rescue plans of her own, to resignation. Her laugh isn’t mockery of God. It is the defensive reflex of someone whom life has taught not to grab hold of hope, because every time she did, she fell. People like that sit in our churches too: they listen to promises with a stony face, not because they despise God, but because they have been burned by waiting too many times. It is worth looking at them the way this story portrays Sarah: without condemnation.

The Guest heard a laugh that made no sound. That is how the hosts recognize who is sitting at their table: not by a miracle, but by the fact that He knows the thoughts locked inside a person. And here is a detail that is easy to miss and that says more about God than many a psalm. Sarah thought, “After I am worn out and my master is old, will I now have this pleasure?” In Hebrew, she describes herself with a word used for a worn, threadbare garment. When God repeats her thought to Abraham, all He says is: “Can I really bear a child when I am old?” “Worn out” disappears, and so does the remark about her husband’s age. God speaks of us more gently than we speak of ourselves. If only one sentence from today’s reading is to stay with you, let it be that one.

sections.heading: Is Anything Too Difficult for the LORD?
paragraphs: God answers Sarah’s laugh with a question: “Is anything too difficult for the LORD?” That question runs through the whole Bible. It gets no answer in this scene, because Sarah, frightened, denies it: “I did not laugh.” And the Guest closes the conversation in a few words: “No… but you did laugh.”

The question itself, meanwhile, sets out on a long journey through Scripture. God will put it to Jeremiah when He tells him to buy a field in a city under siege. And centuries later, announcing another impossible birth, the angel will tell a young girl from Nazareth that nothing is impossible with God. The annunciation in Nazareth quotes the scene under the oaks of Mamre. Every time God announces something impossible, the echo of that noon and that laugh returns.

The words “No… but you did laugh” sound like being caught out, but they are a promise. God doesn’t correct the record to shame Sarah. He refuses to accept her denial because that laugh holds the whole truth about her, and He intends to work with the truth, not with the official version. Since you laughed against hope, you will give birth against nature. God doesn’t reject Sarah because her faith wavered, and He doesn’t take back the promise. Her real, wounded laugh is enough for Him. He takes the rest upon Himself.

sections.heading: The LORD Attended to Sarah
paragraphs: Chapter twenty-one opens with a sentence in which every word is underlined: “Now the LORD attended to Sarah as He had said, and the LORD did for Sarah what He had promised.” As He had said, what He had promised: the same thing stressed twice in a single verse. The narrator can’t stop repeating it. The Lord delayed for a quarter of a century, but He never forgot.

The Hebrew verb translated here as “attended to” literally means visited, looked in on, took up someone’s cause. The same word will later describe the moment when God takes up Israel’s cause in their slavery in Egypt. We already know this pattern from the story of Noah: when God remembers, action follows. With God there isn’t even a crack between “remembered” and “did.”

Then come five verses of dry record: she conceived, she bore, he named, he circumcised, Abraham was a hundred years old. After this report Sarah exclaims, “God has made me laugh.” And she asks, “Who would have told Abraham that Sarah would nurse children?” The answer is: no one. No one except God, and He said it twice before it happened.

There is a simple principle in this that is worth remembering: God doesn’t feed people empty promises, and He is as dependable in keeping them as He was generous in making them. A lot of time may pass between His word and His deed. But nothing stands in the way.

The boy is named Isaac, in Hebrew, “he laughs.” God chose that name, not the parents. Notice what that means in practice. For the rest of her life, every time Sarah calls her son to dinner, she will say a word that reminds her of that laugh behind the tent flap. God didn’t erase her unbelief or order her to forget it. He transformed it: the same laugh that had been despair became joy. God rarely deletes our past. Far more often He gives it a new meaning.

sections.heading: One Son and One Well
paragraphs: Let’s sum up Abraham’s life. Twenty-five years after his call, all he has to show for the great promises is one son and a hard-won right to one well in Beersheba. The nation numbers one child; the promised land, one well shaft. From the outside it looks like failure. And what does the patriarch do? “Abraham planted a tamarisk tree in Beersheba, and there he called upon the name of the LORD, the Eternal God.”

That well is a lesson too. Abraham won the right to it not through a revelation, but through a dispute with his neighbor Abimelech, settled by talking and an oath. Life with a promise isn’t made up of nothing but divine appearances. It consists mostly of long, ordinary years spent with flocks, children, and wells. God leads through those years too, only more quietly. And the most interesting sentence in that story is spoken by a pagan. Abimelech says to Abraham, “God is with you in all that you do.” A Philistine king blesses the man through whom the nations are to be blessed, and doesn’t even know it. The promise is already at work, just quietly.

A man who has lived in tents all his life plants a tree. The tamarisk grows slowly and will give shade only to the generations to come. An old man past a hundred plants a tree he himself will never enjoy, and calls God the Eternal. It is a confession of faith made with a shovel, not with the lips: the future exists, the promise has a sequel, God will be faithful even when I am gone. Sometimes hope looks exactly like that. Not like fireworks, but like a seedling in dry ground.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: God came to people who had run out of possibilities, and He ate dinner with them. He heard the laugh of unbelief and wasn’t offended by it. He quoted a weary woman more gently than she spoke of herself. And then He did exactly what He had promised, and even had the child named “laughter,” so that no one in that house would pretend the unbelief had never happened. If your possibilities have just run out, that is not the end of the story. In this story, at exactly this point, God is only getting started.
